prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five frames show the camera wearer inside a vehicle, with nearby seats, dashboard, roof and windows enclosing the foreground and parked cars distributed outside several metres away. The bright depth regions place the closest people and seat surfaces roughly 0.3–1.2 m from the camera, while the windows and exterior cars are generally about 3–15 m away; the nearby person shifts from the right side in frames 1–2 to near the centre-right in frame 3 as the viewpoint turns, then leaves view in frames 4–5. The map makes foreground–background separation and the relative nearness of the person, seats and dashboard clearer than RGB, including surfaces partly occluding the windows. Absolute metre estimates are uncertain because the monocular map has broad, inconsistent tones, weak exterior detail and apparent depth discontinuities around people, windows and reflective vehicle surfaces.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks identify nearby people, many parked cars outside, a chair/seat in frame 3, and a broad vehicle-related foreground region in frame 5, clarifying which overlapping shapes are separate instances. In frames 1–3, people occupy the near foreground about 0.3–1.2 m away, mainly to the right or centre-right of the camera wearer, while cars seen through the windows are separated into multiple instances roughly 3–15 m away and several metres from one another. The nearby people partly occlude the seats and windows, some bodies are cut off by the bottom or right image boundaries, and the viewpoint turns toward the windshield in frames 4–5 so the people largely disappear while exterior cars spread across the front view. The map is unreliable where large image regions are labelled as single cars, several masks merge with interior surfaces, tiny distant cars receive fragmented or duplicated labels, and it provides no dependable metric depth or facing direction by itself.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only one partial body skeleton in frame 2, located near the centre-right of that frame and corresponding to a nearby person roughly 0.5–1 m in front of and to the right of the camera wearer. Its visible joints form a narrow, partly side-on upper-body/arm configuration, but the missing head and torso detail does not reliably establish whether the person faces or looks toward the camera; no hand skeletons are detected. The detected arm joints appear within that person's own reach and possibly within the camera wearer's arm's reach, while the rest of the body is occluded, cropped or not detected, and no relative geometry between multiple people is available. The pose map exposes articulated joint placement that is difficult to isolate in RGB, but it is highly incomplete and unreliable across time because frames 1 and 3 contain visible people with no skeletons and frames 4–5 contain no usable pose detections.
